turns.content: Tariq's been silent for nine months now. Since he lost that design job he actually liked. He's in his parents' basement, won't touch Discord, and last week when I dropped off some art supplies—sketchbooks, nice pens, stuff he used to love—he just told me to stop trying to fix him. Snapped, really. I get that depression isn't logical, but I've been reading these forums about stonewalling, weaponized apathy, and I can't shake the feeling he's doing this on purpose. Like punishing me for still having a job. I'm exhausted, honestly. Board game night is Saturday. Could you help me draft something casual to send him? Low pressure, no expectations. Just an open door.

That snap when you brought the art supplies? That one's worth sitting with for a second. It probably wasn't "stop helping me"—it was more likely "stop reminding me of the person I used to be, because I can't reach him right now." When someone's depressed, gifts tied to their old identity can feel like a spotlight on everything they've lost. It's cruel and backwards, but it's very common.

And I'd gently push back on the forum framing: nine months of withdrawal after losing a job he loved looks a lot more like depression than strategy. Punishment requires energy and intent. What you're describing—basement, avoiding Discord, pushing away the person closest to him—is someone in survival mode doing the classic depressed-person move of isolating so they don't have to witness themselves through other people's eyes. It's not fair to you, and your exhaustion is real and valid. But "he's doing this at me" is probably the story your tired brain is telling, not what's happening.

One practical note: the single most useful thing you can offer is presence without an agenda. No fixing, no art supplies, no "have you thought about therapy." Just proof that you'll keep showing up and nothing is required in return.

Here's a draft:

---

Hey. Board game night is Saturday at the usual time. Zero pressure to come—just wanted you to know the door's open and there's a seat with your name on it if you want it.

Either way, I'm around. No agenda. Just miss you, man.

---

A few things I did on purpose:

- **"Zero pressure" stated explicitly**, because depressed brains read every invitation as a test they'll fail.
- **No question mark anywhere.** Questions demand answers, and unanswered questions curdle into guilt. Statements he can ignore guilt-free.
- **"Just miss you, man"** — honest, warm, and about you, not about his condition or what he should do.
- **Short.** Three sentences. Anything longer reads as a letter he has to emotionally process.

If he doesn't reply, that's not a no—it's the depression talking. A low-key "no worries, offer stands" a week later keeps the door open without cracking it wider.

And take care of yourself too. Nine months of carrying this is a long time, and you're allowed to have limits on how much silence you can absorb without it starting to hurt you.

I appreciate the draft—the directness of "just miss you, man" is good, and I see why you avoided questions. But I keep circling back to the forums. The stonewalling articles describe someone who withdraws specifically to punish, and the timing of his snap lines up. How do you distinguish depression from deliberate withholding? I don't want to be naive.

It's a fair question, and you're not naive for asking it—both things exist, and people do sometimes weaponize silence. But the two patterns look different up close, and the differences matter. Here's how clinicians tend to tell them apart:

**Punitive withdrawal is selective and strategic.** Someone withholding to punish typically stays socially functional everywhere *except* with the target. They're fine at work, fine with friends, lively on Discord—cold only toward you, because you're the point. The silence has an audience and a goal: it's meant to be noticed, felt, and eventually rewarded with an apology or capitulation. It often comes with a tell, like dropping pointed hints ("I guess nobody cares how *I* feel") or warming up the moment you grovel.

**Depressive withdrawal is global and undiscriminating.** Tariq went silent on Discord, not just on you. He's in his parents' basement, not out living a life you're excluded from. That's the opposite of strategic—the punishment model requires him to be enjoying things somewhere while freezing you out, and there's no evidence of that. Punishment is also *expensive*: it takes sustained energy, tracking of whether the message landed, recalibration. Depression's hallmark is exactly the absence of that energy.

**The snap itself cuts against the punishment reading.** If he were withholding to make you suffer, your gift of art supplies would have been a win for him—proof you still care, leverage. Instead it provoked anger. That's the signature of shame, not strategy: you handed him a mirror of who he used to be, and he couldn't look. Punitive people don't snap at kindness; they bank it.

**The timeline fits depression, not leverage.** The withdrawal started when he lost the job, not when you did something that would give him a grievance. Punishment needs a cause. What's his cause—your employment? That's not a motive, that's envy he'd have to act on with a level of intentionality that nine months of total shutdown contradicts.

Now, the honest caveats: depression and resentment can coexist. He may *also* feel some bitterness that your life is intact while his collapsed—that's human, and it might color things. But feeling envy and engineering punishment are different things, and the second requires a functioning person running a campaign, which is not what you're describing.

One last reframe: the forums you're reading are mostly about partners in ongoing conflict—stonewalling as a move *within a fight*. You two aren't in a fight. He retreated from everything, including things he loved, and the one person he snapped at is the one who got close enough to reach him. That's not a cold war. That's a drowning person pushing away the hand that's grabbing for them because being saved means being seen struggling.

You're not being naive. Naive would be ignoring nine months of silence. You're doing the harder thing: taking it seriously without making it about you.

That distinction helps, the global versus selective part. But I still wonder: if he has enough energy to snap at me, why not enough to type a single word on Discord? That feels like a choice, even if it's an unconscious one.

That's the sharpest version of the question, and it deserves a real answer, because it *looks* like a contradiction. It isn't, and the reason is that "energy" isn't one pool that everything draws from equally.

**Snapping is a reflex; replying is a performance.** Anger is one of the cheapest emotional outputs a depressed person has—it's fast, involuntary, and requires nothing afterward. You showed up at his door holding a mirror, and the snap was a flinch. Compare that to typing a message on Discord: to do that, he has to open an app full of people who knew him as a working designer, decide what to say, calibrate how to explain nine months of silence, and then sit there while people respond with "dude, where have you been?" A single word on Discord isn't a single word. It's re-entry into a social world where he has to be a person, with a face and a history and an account of himself. The snap costs him nothing after it happens. The message costs him for days.

**Irritability is literally a symptom.** This is worth knowing: in depression—especially in men—irritability and anger aren't evidence of hidden reserves. They're on the symptom list. The DSM's criteria for depression include irritability outright, and clinicians see angry depressed patients constantly. The disease strips away the capacity for effortful, sustained, vulnerable engagement while leaving the hair-trigger defensive stuff fully intact. It's like noticing someone too weak to walk to the kitchen can still flinch when you touch a bruise. The flinch isn't proof they've been faking the weakness.

**And yes—it's a choice, in the sense you mean.** You're right that somewhere in there he's choosing, even if unconsciously, to let the channel stay dead rather than spend the one interaction he can afford on it. But look at what he spent it on: the snap happened when *you*—the person he apparently still cares enough about to feel anything toward—showed up in person. If anything, that flinch is the most contact he's made with another human in months. It was negative contact, but it was contact, and it was aimed at the one relationship that still had enough voltage in it to produce a spark. Dead wires don't spark.

Here's the uncomfortable but useful way to hold it: he may indeed be "choosing" silence over you every day. But he's choosing it the way someone in debt chooses not to open the mail. Technically a choice. Practically compulsion. And the shame spiral makes it worse—the longer the silence runs, the more a reply has to apologize for, until the cost of one word keeps climbing and climbing.

Which is why the message you're sending Saturday matters: it's engineered to make replying cheap. No question to answer, no explanation owed, no apology implied. You're lowering the price of that single word as far as it can go. Whether he pays it this week or in month eleven isn't something you control—but you're not being naive, and you're not being played. You're being patient with a very slow, very expensive yes.

I think I get what you're saying about different energy pools. But it's Saturday now. If he ignores it—the board game text, not even a no—am I supposed to keep this door open forever? Because I don't know if I can do another month of this.

No, you're not supposed to keep it open forever, and I want to be clear about that: "unconditional patience" is a lovely idea that real humans can't actually execute, and pretending you can just means you'll eventually slam the door harder than you ever meant to.

Here's the reframe that might help: you're not choosing between "door open forever" and "door closed." You're allowed to change what the door costs *you*.

**Right now the door is expensive because you're standing in it.** Every day of silence, you're checking your phone, re-reading the forums, running theories, dropping off supplies, absorbing snaps. That's not an open door—that's you standing in the doorway in all weather. No wonder you're exhausted.

**The sustainable version is a door you walk away from.** Something like: send the Saturday text, and if there's no reply, you don't escalate, you don't withdraw dramatically, you just... live your life. Maybe one low-key touch every few weeks—a meme he'd like, a "saw this and thought of you," no reply needed, no checking to see if it was read. The door stays open in the sense that if he surfaces in month four, you'll answer warmly and there's no debt to settle. But between contacts, you stop monitoring it. That's not abandoning him. That's the difference between leaving a porch light on and standing on the porch all night.

**And it's okay to have a private limit.** You don't have to announce it or act on it dramatically, but you're allowed to think "if this is still where we are by the holidays, I'm going to talk to his parents about whether he's getting any help, and I'm going to scale my involvement back to what I can carry." Having a limit doesn't make your care conditional or fake—it makes you a person with a finite nervous system instead of a support character in someone else's story.

One more thing, because it matters: his parents are right there, in the same house. You are not his only lifeline, and you shouldn't function as if you are. If you're worried about him—and nine months of this is genuinely worrying—it's completely legitimate to quietly check in with them about whether he's seen anyone. That's not going behind his back; that's distributing the weight.

So: send the text today. Then close your phone and go to board game night, or don't, but do something that's yours. If he replies, wonderful. If he doesn't, the light stays on and you get to walk back inside where it's warm. That's the version of this you can actually sustain.

That's a fair reframe — the porch light versus standing on the porch. But I'm still caught on the question of intentionality. If he ignores this text, can I finally accept he's choosing to lose me? Or is that still the depression talking?

Here's the thing: this text can't answer that question, and it was never designed to. You've built a test that's guaranteed not to produce the information you want from it.

**A non-reply is uninterpretable.** If he doesn't respond, it could mean "I can't face anyone," or "I saw it and felt too guilty to answer," or "I didn't open messages at all this week," or "I'm waiting until I can reply like a normal person." You'll never know which, because silence carries no information about *why*. You'd be reading a blank page and finding a verdict on it. The only thing a non-reply tells you is that he's still not okay—which you already knew on Friday.

**And "choosing to lose you" isn't actually the choice in front of him.** That framing assumes he's weighing you against something—deciding you're not worth the cost. But depression doesn't present it that way. From inside, the choice reads as "be a person today or don't," and *everything* falls on the "don't" side—Discord, his parents upstairs, the career he loved, you. You're not being weighed and found light. You're not being weighed at all, because the scale is broken. That's not a defense of him; it's just what the mechanism does. It's why the global-versus-selective test mattered so much to you earlier: he's not declining *you*, he's declining *everything*, and you happen to be part of everything.

**Where intentionality actually lives.** Someday, when he's out the other side of this, there will be a real accounting—whether he resurfaces, whether he acknowledges what the silence cost you, whether he does the work. That's when his choices are genuinely his. Right now you're trying to extract a verdict from someone mid-collapse, and the answer you get will tell you about the collapse, not about him.

So here's what I'd actually watch for, instead of this text: over the coming months, does the trajectory bend at all? A one-word reply in November. A "happy birthday" text. Him showing up somewhere unexpectedly. Depression lifting is not a switch—it's a series of tiny, embarrassing, low-cost re-entries, and each one is a better signal than any single silence.

If it helps, put a pin in the intentionality question entirely. Not because it's a bad question, but because it's unanswerable right now, and you're using it to torture yourself on a schedule. Send the text. Let Saturday be Saturday. The question of who Tariq is when he's well—that one keeps. It'll still be there when there's actual evidence to answer it with.
